herodotus.author: Herodotus
herodotus.note: main narrative; wrote about 50 years after the battle, from Athenian and other informants

aeschylus.author: Aeschylus
aeschylus.note: a play staged 8 years after the battle, for an audience of men who fought in it

facts.claim: The battle of Salamis was fought in 480 BC, traditionally dated to late September.
Xerxes sent a horseman to Susa to announce his success.
Aeschylus, eight years later, also tells of a Greek who came to Xerxes saying the Greeks would slip away under cover of night.
Xerxes watched the battle seated at the foot of Mount Aigaleos, on the mainland opposite Salamis.
Whenever he saw one of his captains do something notable, he asked who it was, and his scribes wrote down the captain's name, his father and his city.
Plutarch says Xerxes sat on a golden throne, with many secretaries beside him to record the battle.
Artemisia, queen of Halicarnassus, chased by an Athenian ship, rammed and sank a ship from her own side.
Xerxes thought she had sunk a Greek ship and said: my men have become women, and my women men.
When Phoenician captains blamed the Ionians for the defeat, Xerxes had them beheaded.
Aeschylus says that when Xerxes saw the depth of the disaster he tore his robes and cried out, for he had a seat in full view of the whole army, on a high hill near the sea.
In the narrow strait the crowded Persian ships could not use their numbers; they struck each other with their bronze rams and broke their oars.

facts.note: Herodotus gives 378 Greek ships; modern historians think the Persian fleet was far smaller than 1,207 by the day of battle. Say 'Aeschylus claims'.
facts.claim: Aeschylus puts the Greek fleet at about 310 ships and Xerxes' fleet at 1,207.
